claim: Sleep benefits consolidation of memories, especially those of motivational relevance.
source: Sleep is known to benefit consolidation of memories, especially those of motivational relevance.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data from this study.

claim: Presenting the spoken name of a familiar, valued snack item during midday nap significantly improves the preference for that item relative to items not externally cued.
source: Specifically, presenting the spoken name of a familiar, valued snack item during midday nap significantly improves the preference for that item relative to items not externally cued.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from the BDM auction and binary choice tasks.

claim: The cueing-specific preference enhancement is sleep-dependent.
source: The cueing-specific preference enhancement is sleep-dependent and can be predicted by cue-induced neurophysiological signals at the subject and item level.
evidence: This is supported by comparing sleep and wake groups, showing effects only in the sleep group.

claim: The cueing-specific preference enhancement can be predicted by cue-induced neurophysiological signals at the subject and item level.
source: The cueing-specific preference enhancement is sleep-dependent and can be predicted by cue-induced neurophysiological signals at the subject and item level.
evidence: This is supported by EEG data showing correlations between delta/theta power and preference changes.

claim: Sleep cueing accelerates evidence accumulation for cued options during the post-sleep choice process in a manner consistent with the preference shift.
source: Computational modeling further suggests that sleep cueing accelerates evidence accumulation for cued options during the post-sleep choice process in a manner consistent with the preference shift.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling using the LBA model showing higher drift rates for cued items.

claim: Neurocognitive processing during sleep contributes to the fine-tuning of subjective preferences in a flexible, selective manner.
source: These findings suggest that neurocognitive processing during sleep contributes to the fine-tuning of subjective preferences in a flexible, selective manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings of the study.

claim: Spontaneous neural activation has been observed in the ventral striatum during sleep.
source: Spontaneous neural activation has been observed in the ventral striatum (Peigneux et al., 2004; Pennartz et al., 2004; Lansink et al., 2008; Lansink et al., 2009) and other brain structures implicated in reward processing (Cantero et al., 2003; Schabus et al., 2007; Singer and Frank, 2009; Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The engagement of reward circuits during sleep has been postulated to promote the consolidation of reward-related information.
source: This engagement of reward circuits has been postulated to promote the consolidation of reward-related information (Pennartz et al., 2004; Fischer and Born, 2009; Pennartz et al., 2011), and prioritize information of high motivational saliency for sleep-dependent reprocessing (Fischer and Born, 2009; Sterpenich et al., 2009; Wilhelm et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Choosing among different options involves computing a subjective value for each option and comparing these values to make a decision.
source: Choosing among different options involves computing a subjective value for each option and comparing these values to make a decision (Samuelson, 1938; Rangel and Hare, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in decision-making research supported by citations.

claim: Subjective preferences are not formed once and forever, but can be modulated by external and internal factors in the waking state.
source: Indeed, extant data have demonstrated that subjective preferences are not formed once and forever, but can be modulated by external (e.g. reward reinforcement (Tobler et al., 2005)) and internal factors in the waking state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Memory retrieval has been shown to influence the weighting of choice options in certain types of decisions.
source: For example, memory retrieval has been shown to influence the weighting of choice options in certain types of decisions (Barron et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2015; Bornstein and Norman, 2017), whereas attention affects the comparison of choice values in a range of economic behaviors (Armel et al., 2008; Krajbich et al., 2010; Schonberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Attention affects the comparison of choice values in a range of economic behaviors.
source: For example, memory retrieval has been shown to influence the weighting of choice options in certain types of decisions (Barron et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2015; Bornstein and Norman, 2017), whereas attention affects the comparison of choice values in a range of economic behaviors (Armel et al., 2008; Krajbich et al., 2010; Schonberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Targeted memory reactivation has been shown effective in selectively improving post-sleep performances in spatial memory.
source: The method has been shown effective in selectively improving post-sleep performances in a range of cognitive tasks, including spatial memory (Rasch et al., 2007; Rudoy et al., 2009; Diekelmann et al., 2011), motor memory (Antony et al., 2012), vocabulary learning (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015; Schreiner and Rasch, 2017; Tamminen et al., 2017), fear extinction (Hauner et al., 2013; He et al., 2015), and the reduction of implicit social biases (Hu et al., 2015), but its influence on value-based decisions has yet to be explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous TMR studies.

claim: Targeted memory reactivation has been shown effective in selectively improving post-sleep performances in motor memory.
source: The method has been shown effective in selectively improving post-sleep performances in a range of cognitive tasks, including spatial memory (Rasch et al., 2007; Rudoy et al., 2009; Diekelmann et al., 2011), motor memory (Antony et al., 2012), vocabulary learning (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015; Schreiner and Rasch, 2017; Tamminen et al., 2017), fear extinction (Hauner et al., 2013; He et al., 2015), and the reduction of implicit social biases (Hu et al., 2015), but its influence on value-based decisions has yet to be explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous TMR studies.

claim: Targeted memory reactivation has been shown effective in selectively improving post-sleep performances in vocabulary learning.
source: The method has been shown effective in selectively improving post-sleep performances in a range of cognitive tasks, including spatial memory (Rasch et al., 2007; Rudoy et al., 2009; Diekelmann et al., 2011), motor memory (Antony et al., 2012), vocabulary learning (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015; Schreiner and Rasch, 2017; Tamminen et al., 2017), fear extinction (Hauner et al., 2013; He et al., 2015), and the reduction of implicit social biases (Hu et al., 2015), but its influence on value-based decisions has yet to be explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous TMR studies.

claim: Targeted memory reactivation has been shown effective in fear extinction.
source: The method has been shown effective in selectively improving post-sleep performances in a range of cognitive tasks, including spatial memory (Rasch et al., 2007; Rudoy et al., 2009; Diekelmann et al., 2011), motor memory (Antony et al., 2012), vocabulary learning (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015; Schreiner and Rasch, 2017; Tamminen et al., 2017), fear extinction (Hauner et al., 2013; He et al., 2015), and the reduction of implicit social biases (Hu et al., 2015), but its influence on value-based decisions has yet to be explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous TMR studies.

claim: Targeted memory reactivation has been shown effective in the reduction of implicit social biases.
source: The method has been shown effective in selectively improving post-sleep performances in a range of cognitive tasks, including spatial memory (Rasch et al., 2007; Rudoy et al., 2009; Diekelmann et al., 2011), motor memory (Antony et al., 2012), vocabulary learning (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015; Schreiner and Rasch, 2017; Tamminen et al., 2017), fear extinction (Hauner et al., 2013; He et al., 2015), and the reduction of implicit social biases (Hu et al., 2015), but its influence on value-based decisions has yet to be explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous TMR studies.

claim: The study tested 92 healthy adults.
source: We tested 92 healthy adults (Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1, Table 1A for demographic information) in a battery of classic simple economic choice experiments in combination with the TMR procedure (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample size.

claim: Subjects were introduced to a set of 60 familiar snack items with self-reported familiarity rating of 3.51 ± 0.84 on a 5-point scale.
source: Subjects were first introduced to a set of 60 familiar snack items (self-reported familiarity rating = 3.51 ± 0.84, on a 5-point scale, Supplementary file 1, Table 1B), and indicated their willingness-to-pay (WTP) in a Becker-DeGroot-Marschak (BDM) auction (Becker et al., 1964), which served as a measure of the baseline preference for a snack item (henceforth WTP1) (Plassmann et al., 2007; Hare et al., 2008; Schonberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: Eight pairs of snacks were chosen for each subject that were matched by baseline preferences and randomly divided into cued and uncued conditions.
source: On the basis of WTP1, we chose eight pairs of snacks for each subject that were matched by baseline preferences and randomly divided into cued and uncued conditions.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: During sleep, the names of eight snack items were delivered over a speaker, each for ten repetitions, during N2 sleep with no sleep disruption.
source: During subsequent sleep (sleep group, N = 47), the names of eight snack items (i.e. cued items) were delivered over a speaker, each for ten repetitions, during the stage 2 of non-rapid eye movement (N2) sleep with no sleep disruption (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015; Cairney et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The baseline ΔWTP for items that had not been cued was not significantly different from zero in either subject group.
source: Consistent with previous evidence that WTP reliably reflects the subjective value of a familiar option (Plassmann et al., 2007), the baseline ΔWTP (i.e. ΔWTP for items that had not been cued) was not significantly different from zero in either subject group (all subjects, ΔWTP = 0.11 ± 0.12, t91 = 0.99, p = 0.323; sleep vs. wake, t90 = - 0.97, p = 0.336), suggesting the test-and-retest stability of preferences for snack items examined in our experiment.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant main effect in ΔWTP between the sleep and wake groups.
source: Using ΔWTP, we found that there was no significant main effect in ΔWTP between the sleep and wake groups (sleep: 0.29 ± 0.12; wake: 0.32 ± 0.11; main effect in cohort, F1,90 = 0.02, p = 0.886; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant within-subject difference associated with cueing, such that previously cued items were associated with higher ΔWTP relative to uncued items.
source: On the other hand, there was a significant within-subject difference associated with cueing, such that previously cued items were associated with higher ΔWTP relative to uncued items (cued: 0.50 ± 0.11; uncued: 0.11 ± 0.12; main effect in cueing condition, F1,90 = 27.61, p = 9.9 × 10−7; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ΔWTP was significantly higher for cued relative to uncued items in the sleep group but not in the wake group.
source: Importantly, cue-induced effects on preferences varied between sleep and wake cohorts as predicted: ΔWTP was significantly higher for cued relative to uncued items in the sleep group but not in the wake group ((cued vs. uncued) × (sleep vs. wake): F1,90 = 6.95, p = 0.01; Figure 2A), suggesting that verbal cueing during sleep but not wakefulness promotes preferences for previously cued items.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Verbal cueing during sleep but not wakefulness promotes preferences for previously cued items.
source: Importantly, cue-induced effects on preferences varied between sleep and wake cohorts as predicted: ΔWTP was significantly higher for cued relative to uncued items in the sleep group but not in the wake group ((cued vs. uncued) × (sleep vs. wake): F1,90 = 6.95, p = 0.01; Figure 2A), suggesting that verbal cueing during sleep but not wakefulness promotes preferences for previously cued items.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical findings.

claim: Relative to WTP1, cueing during sleep promotes preferences by 8.3% (±1.3%) for cued items more than for items not externally cued.
source: Relative to WTP1 (¥7.02 ± ¥0.16), cueing during sleep promotes preferences by 8.3% (±1.3%) for cued items more than for items not externally cued, whereas during wakefulness cueing increases WTP by 3.5% (±2.1%) for cued relative to uncued items.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2A.

claim: During wakefulness cueing increases WTP by 3.5% (±2.1%) for cued relative to uncued items.
source: Relative to WTP1 (¥7.02 ± ¥0.16), cueing during sleep promotes preferences by 8.3% (±1.3%) for cued items more than for items not externally cued, whereas during wakefulness cueing increases WTP by 3.5% (±2.1%) for cued relative to uncued items.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2A.

claim: The choice distribution of the sleep group significantly skewed toward cued items.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that the choice distribution of the sleep group significantly skewed toward cued items (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Z = - 4.45, p = 8.4 × 10−6; Figure 2B), indicating a behavioral bias favoring items previously named during sleep.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Choices of the wake group were distributed almost symmetrically around the chance level.
source: In stark contrast, choices of the wake group were distributed almost symmetrically around the chance level (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Z = - 0.88, p = 0.379), indicating that the same verbal stimulation during wakefulness did not alter preferences for cued over uncued items.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Sleep group subjects were more likely to select items that were previously cued than wake group participants (sleep: 59.4 ± 1.6%; wake: 52.5 ± 2.5%).
source: On average, sleep group subjects were more likely to select items that were previously cued than wake group participants (sleep: 59.4 ± 1.6%; wake: 52.5 ± 2.5%; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Z = 2.63, p = 0.009; Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1, Table 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: WTP2 differences predicted the choice behavior in both sleep and wake groups.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Sugrue et al., 2005), WTP2 differences predicted the choice behavior in both sleep and wake groups (sleep: r = 0.37, p = 0.011; wake: r = 0.39, p = 0.009), whereas WTP1 differences had no predictive power for the choice behavior in either subject group (sleep: r = 0.01, p = 0.945; wake: r = 0.05, p = 0.746).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of the data.

claim: WTP1 differences had no predictive power for the choice behavior in either subject group.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Sugrue et al., 2005), WTP2 differences predicted the choice behavior in both sleep and wake groups (sleep: r = 0.37, p = 0.011; wake: r = 0.39, p = 0.009), whereas WTP1 differences had no predictive power for the choice behavior in either subject group (sleep: r = 0.01, p = 0.945; wake: r = 0.05, p = 0.746).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of the data.

claim: The regression results showed no significant differences in slopes between the sleep and wake cohorts.
source: In contrast to this prediction, the regression results showed no significant differences in slopes between the sleep and wake cohorts (sleep = 0.06; wake = 0.08; F1,88 = 0.19, p = 0.665).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of regression slopes.

claim: Differences were found only in the intercepts between sleep and wake groups (sleep = 0.56, wake = 0.51).
source: Differences were found only in the intercepts (sleep = 0.56, wake = 0.51, F1,88 = 6.34, p = 0.014; Figure 3A), suggesting that the behavioral differences between sleep and wake protocols could not be attributed to differential choice randomness but rather to an overall shift in choice propensity toward cued items under the sleep protocol.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The behavioral differences between sleep and wake protocols could not be attributed to differential choice randomness but rather to an overall shift in choice propensity toward cued items under the sleep protocol.
source: Differences were found only in the intercepts (sleep = 0.56, wake = 0.51, F1,88 = 6.34, p = 0.014; Figure 3A), suggesting that the behavioral differences between sleep and wake protocols could not be attributed to differential choice randomness but rather to an overall shift in choice propensity toward cued items under the sleep protocol.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: A cue-evoked neural response was observed at the frontal electrode sites during N2 sleep, characterized by a positive ERP around 450 ms followed by a negative peak around 1000 ms.
source: By averaging ERP amplitudes measured over the interval from −200 to 1800 ms with respect to the onset of each verbal cue, we observed a cue-evoked neural response at the frontal electrode sites (representative electrode F3) during N2 sleep (Figure 4A). Characterized by a positive ERP around 450 ms followed by a negative peak around 1000 ms, this observed pattern is similar to the well-established waveform of K-complexes (KCs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1, Table 1F) (Niiyama et al., 1995; Cote et al., 1999; Blume et al., 2017), an electroencephalogram (EEG) graphoelement that has been repeatedly associated with the processing of sensory stimuli, including auditory cues, mainly during periods identified as N2 (Halász, 2005; Cash et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by EEG data analysis and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The observed ERP pattern is similar to the well-established waveform of K-complexes.
source: Characterized by a positive ERP around 450 ms followed by a negative peak around 1000 ms, this observed pattern is similar to the well-established waveform of K-complexes (KCs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1, Table 1F) (Niiyama et al., 1995; Cote et al., 1999; Blume et al., 2017), an electroencephalogram (EEG) graphoelement that has been repeatedly associated with the processing of sensory stimuli, including auditory cues, mainly during periods identified as N2 (Halász, 2005; Cash et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with established literature and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Presentation of verbal stimuli elicited no significant increase in high-frequency activity (8–35 Hz).
source: We observed no significant increase in high-frequency activity (8–35 Hz), which would have been observed if verbal stimuli had reduced the depth of sleep in participants (Figure 4A) (Ruch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis of EEG data and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no significant change in alpha, beta, or gamma bands after stimulus presentation.
source: More specifically, by contrasting the mean spectral power for high-frequency bands before and after the stimulus presentation, we found no significant change for the alpha, beta, or gamma bands (alpha: t22 = - 1.51, p = 0.728; beta: t22 = - 1.68, p = 0.535; gamma: t22 = - 0.23, p = 1; all Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of spectral power.

claim: Presentation of verbal stimuli elicited strong event-related synchronization for low-frequency activity (0.5–8 Hz), including the delta band.
source: In sharp contrast, presentation of verbal stimuli elicited strong event-related synchronization for low-frequency activity (0.5–8 Hz), including the delta band (t22 = - 6.88, p = 3.3 × 10−6) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which has been previously implicated in the detection of motivationally salient stimuli (Blume et al., 2017) and improved memory consolidation (Oudiette et al., 2013; Batterink et al., 2016), and the theta band (t22 = - 7.13, p = 1.9 × 10−6), which has been associated with memory processing during wakefulness (Lisman and Jensen, 2013) and successful cueing during non-rapid eye movement sleep in both healthy (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015) and patient (Hot et al., 2011) populations.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Presentation of verbal stimuli elicited strong event-related synchronization for the theta band.
source: In sharp contrast, presentation of verbal stimuli elicited strong event-related synchronization for low-frequency activity (0.5–8 Hz), including the delta band (t22 = - 6.88, p = 3.3 × 10−6) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which has been previously implicated in the detection of motivationally salient stimuli (Blume et al., 2017) and improved memory consolidation (Oudiette et al., 2013; Batterink et al., 2016), and the theta band (t22 = - 7.13, p = 1.9 × 10−6), which has been associated with memory processing during wakefulness (Lisman and Jensen, 2013) and successful cueing during non-rapid eye movement sleep in both healthy (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015) and patient (Hot et al., 2011) populations.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Among sleep group subjects, individuals associated with more prominent increases in average delta band power later demonstrated more pronounced post-sleep preference enhancements for cued items (r = 0.65, p = 0.005).
source: That is, among the sleep group subjects, individuals associated with more prominent increases in average delta or theta band power later demonstrated more pronounced post-sleep preference enhancements for cued items (delta: r = 0.65, p = 0.005; theta: r = 0.64, p = 0.004; all Bonferroni corrected; Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Among sleep group subjects, individuals associated with more prominent increases in average theta band power later demonstrated more pronounced post-sleep preference enhancements for cued items (r = 0.64, p = 0.004).
source: That is, among the sleep group subjects, individuals associated with more prominent increases in average delta or theta band power later demonstrated more pronounced post-sleep preference enhancements for cued items (delta: r = 0.65, p = 0.005; theta: r = 0.64, p = 0.004; all Bonferroni corrected; Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Among items that had been presented during sleep, those associated with more prominent increases in average delta band power showed greater post-sleep improvement in WTP (r = 0.52, p = 0.001).
source: Similarly, among items that had been presented during sleep, those associated with more prominent increases in average delta or theta band power showed greater post-sleep improvement in WTP (delta: r = 0.52, p = 0.001; theta: r = 0.47, p = 0.005; all Bonferroni corrected; Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Among items that had been presented during sleep, those associated with more prominent increases in average theta band power showed greater post-sleep improvement in WTP (r = 0.47, p = 0.005).
source: Similarly, among items that had been presented during sleep, those associated with more prominent increases in average delta or theta band power showed greater post-sleep improvement in WTP (delta: r = 0.52, p = 0.001; theta: r = 0.47, p = 0.005; all Bonferroni corrected; Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There was no correlation between the post-sleep change in preference for cued items and the changes in power in the alpha, beta, or gamma bands.
source: In contrast, there was no correlation between the post-sleep change in preference for cued items and the changes in power in the alpha, beta, or gamma bands (alpha: p = 0.463; beta: p = 1; gamma: p = 1; Bonferroni corrected; Supplementary file 1, Table 1G).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: The LBA model explained RT and choice behavior very well, with observed choices and RT highly correlated with predictions based on model estimation (RT: r = 0.995; choices: r = 0.984).
source: Results based on a hierarchical Bayesian model estimation (Gelman et al., 2014) suggested that LBA explained RT and choice behavior very well: the observed choices and RT were highly correlated with predictions based on model estimation, with both correlation coefficients close to 1 (RT: r = 0.995, p = 2.2 × 10−16; choices: r = 0.984, p = 2.2 × 10−16; Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and no significant difference in the explanatory power between sleep and wake groups (RT: rsleep = 0.992, rwake = 0.997, F1,88 = 0.42, p = 0.52; choices: rsleep = 0.973, rwake = 0.988, F1,88 = 0.50, p = 0.480).
evidence: This is supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant difference in the explanatory power of the LBA model between sleep and wake groups.
source: Results based on a hierarchical Bayesian model estimation (Gelman et al., 2014) suggested that LBA explained RT and choice behavior very well: the observed choices and RT were highly correlated with predictions based on model estimation, with both correlation coefficients close to 1 (RT: r = 0.995, p = 2.2 × 10−16; choices: r = 0.984, p = 2.2 × 10−16; Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and no significant difference in the explanatory power between sleep and wake groups (RT: rsleep = 0.992, rwake = 0.997, F1,88 = 0.42, p = 0.52; choices: rsleep = 0.973, rwake = 0.988, F1,88 = 0.50, p = 0.480).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of model fits.

claim: There was no significant main effect in the drift rate between sleep and wake groups.
source: Consistent with the ΔWTP pattern shown in Figure 2A, we found no significant main effect in the drift rate between sleep and wake groups (sleep = 3.17 ± 0.06; wake = 3.17 ± 0.07; main effect in treatment, F1,90 = 0, p = 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), yet a significant within-subject difference between cued and uncued items, such that previously cued items were associated with higher drift rates (cued = 3.37 ± 0.06; uncued = 2.96 ± 0.06; main effect in cueing condition, F1,90 = 25.26, p = 2.53 × 10−6).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of LBA model parameters shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There was a significant within-subject difference between cued and uncued items, such that previously cued items were associated with higher drift rates.
source: Consistent with the ΔWTP pattern shown in Figure 2A, we found no significant main effect in the drift rate between sleep and wake groups (sleep = 3.17 ± 0.06; wake = 3.17 ± 0.07; main effect in treatment, F1,90 = 0, p = 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), yet a significant within-subject difference between cued and uncued items, such that previously cued items were associated with higher drift rates (cued = 3.37 ± 0.06; uncued = 2.96 ± 0.06; main effect in cueing condition, F1,90 = 25.26, p = 2.53 × 10−6).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of LBA model parameters shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The drift rate was significantly higher for cued relative to uncued items in the sleep but not wake group.
source: Importantly, the cue-induced effect on drift rate varied between sleep and wake groups in a manner consistent with the pattern of ΔWTP: the drift rate was significantly higher for cued relative to uncued items in the sleep but not wake group ((cued vs. uncued) × (sleep vs. wake): F1,90 = 5.29, p = 0.024), suggesting that stimulating the sleeping brain selectively accelerated the drifting process for cued items during the subsequent decision.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of LBA model parameters.

claim: Stimulating the sleeping brain selectively accelerated the drifting process for cued items during the subsequent decision.
source: Importantly, the cue-induced effect on drift rate varied between sleep and wake groups in a manner consistent with the pattern of ΔWTP: the drift rate was significantly higher for cued relative to uncued items in the sleep but not wake group ((cued vs. uncued) × (sleep vs. wake): F1,90 = 5.29, p = 0.024), suggesting that stimulating the sleeping brain selectively accelerated the drifting process for cued items during the subsequent decision.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the drift rate findings.

claim: Individuals with stronger biases towards cued items in WTP2 demonstrated a more pronounced increment in the drift rate from uncued to cued items (r = 0.37, p = 0.001).
source: Across subjects, the extent to which evidence accumulated faster for cued relative to uncued items can be predicted by the degree of preference bias toward cued items. Specifically, individuals with stronger biases towards cued items in WTP2 demonstrated a more pronounced increment in the drift rate from uncued to cued items (r = 0.37, p = 0.001; Figure 4—figure supplement 4A), with no significant difference in the correlation coefficient across cohorts (sleep: r = 0.35; wake: r = 0.28; F1,88 = 0.50, p = 0.48).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Within sleep group participants, the drift rate estimate was correlated with brain activity measured during N2.
source: Within sleep group participants, the drift rate estimate was also correlated with brain activity measured during N2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Sleep exerted no general influence on parameters directly related to valuation, such as drift rate, starting-point variability, and decision threshold.
source: Whereas sleep exerted no general influence on parameters directly related to valuation, such as drift rate, starting-point variability, and decision threshold (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), sleep slowed down the cognitive processing that was unrelated to decision.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of LBA model parameters shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The sleep group was associated with a longer non-decision time relative to the wake group (sleep = 0.72 ± 0.01; wake = 0.61 ± 0.01).
source: Relative to the wake group, the sleep group was associated with a longer non-decision time (sleep = 0.72 ± 0.01; wake = 0.61 ± 0.01; t = 5.71, p = 7.23 × 10−7; Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), a parameter that captures individual differences in RT affected by cognitive factors separated from valuation (e.g. visual or motor processing).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of LBA model parameters shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Subjects who stayed awake for 90 min felt hungrier than those who took a nap (post-stimulation self-reported hunger in the sleep group = 4.79 ± 0.29; wake group = 5.66 ± 0.26).
source: A likely reason for the swift non-decision process in the wake group is that subjects who stayed awake for 90 min felt hungrier than those who took a nap (post-stimulation self-reported hunger in the sleep group = 4.79 ± 0.29; wake group = 5.66 ± 0.26; t = - 2.26, p = 0.026; Supplementary file 1, Table 1A).
evidence: This is supported by self-report data.

claim: Non-decision time estimates were scaled with the change of self-reported hunger before and after 90-min period at the across-subject level (r = 0.27, p = 0.009).
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, non-decision time estimates were scaled with the change of self-reported hunger before and after 90-min period at the across-subject level (r = 0.27, p = 0.009; Figure 4—figure supplement 4C), with no significant difference in the correlation coefficient between cohorts (sleep = 0.51; wake = 0.48; F = 0.23, p = 0.633).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

claim: There was no correlation between the non-decision time estimates and the change in vigilance, the familiarity of items, or demographic variables.
source: In contrast, there was no correlation between the non-decision time estimates and the change in vigilance, the familiarity of items, or demographic variables (all p>0.5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Preference enhancement following sleep TMR results from neurocognitive processing of verbal stimuli during sleep, as indexed by the power of low-frequency bands evoked by verbal cues.
source: These results suggest that preference modification following sleep TMR results from neurocognitive processing of verbal stimuli during sleep, as indexed by the power of low-frequency bands evoked by verbal cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EEG findings.

claim: The stimulation effect is sleep-dependent and stimulation in the waking state produces no significant changes in preferences or choices.
source: The fact that the stimulation effect is sleep-dependent and that cueing in the waking state produces no significant changes in preferences or choices is consistent with past evidence that selective memory reactivation during wakefulness does not always improve memory (Rudoy et al., 2009; Antony et al., 2012; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015) and sometimes even produces opposing consequences (Diekelmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: Selective memory reactivation during wakefulness does not always improve memory and sometimes even produces opposing consequences.
source: The fact that the stimulation effect is sleep-dependent and that cueing in the waking state produces no significant changes in preferences or choices is consistent with past evidence that selective memory reactivation during wakefulness does not always improve memory (Rudoy et al., 2009; Antony et al., 2012; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015) and sometimes even produces opposing consequences (Diekelmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The degree of post-sleep preference enhancement can be predicted by cue-induced increases of theta or delta power.
source: Importantly, and consistent with previous studies (Antony et al., 2012; Oudiette et al., 2013; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015), the degree of post-sleep preference enhancement can be predicted by cue-induced increases of theta or delta power, which have been previously associated with successful cueing during sleep (Schreiner et al., 2015; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015) and with improved memory consolidation (Oudiette et al., 2013; Batterink et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the EEG data and citations to previous research.

claim: Theta and delta power have been previously associated with successful cueing during sleep.
source: Importantly, and consistent with previous studies (Antony et al., 2012; Oudiette et al., 2013; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015), the degree of post-sleep preference enhancement can be predicted by cue-induced increases of theta or delta power, which have been previously associated with successful cueing during sleep (Schreiner et al., 2015; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015) and with improved memory consolidation (Oudiette et al., 2013; Batterink et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Delta power has been previously associated with improved memory consolidation.
source: Importantly, and consistent with previous studies (Antony et al., 2012; Oudiette et al., 2013; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015), the degree of post-sleep preference enhancement can be predicted by cue-induced increases of theta or delta power, which have been previously associated with successful cueing during sleep (Schreiner et al., 2015; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015) and with improved memory consolidation (Oudiette et al., 2013; Batterink et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sleep contributes to the dynamic nature of preferences in a flexible, selective manner, such that preferences for specific options can be individually biased during sleep.
source: Our findings corroborate a wealth of evidence suggesting that subjective preferences interact dynamically with the environmental and cognitive states of a decision-maker, and extend these previous findings by demonstrating that sleep also contributes to the dynamic nature of preferences in a flexible, selective manner, such that preferences for specific options can be individually biased during sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Preference reflects the outcome of memory retrieval, and verbal cueing during sleep encourages the preference of a familiar, valued item by reactivating and strengthening the relevant memories.
source: Under this interpretation, preference reflects the outcome of memory retrieval, and verbal cueing during sleep encourages the preference of a familiar, valued item by reactivating and strengthening the relevant memories.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Important memories, including those of motivational salience, are preferentially reactivated during sleep.
source: In keeping with this possibility, previous studies have suggested that important memories, including those of motivational salience, are preferentially reactivated during sleep (Lansink et al., 2008; Dunsmoor et al., 2015; Blume et al., 2017) and that successful retrieval of a relevant episodic memory (e.g. a past action (Bornstein et al., 2017) or contextual information associated with an action (Bornstein and Norman, 2017)) leads to subsequent decision biases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Successful retrieval of a relevant episodic memory leads to subsequent decision biases.
source: In keeping with this possibility, previous studies have suggested that important memories, including those of motivational salience, are preferentially reactivated during sleep (Lansink et al., 2008; Dunsmoor et al., 2015; Blume et al., 2017) and that successful retrieval of a relevant episodic memory (e.g. a past action (Bornstein et al., 2017) or contextual information associated with an action (Bornstein and Norman, 2017)) leads to subsequent decision biases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The interplay between memory and choice processes involves a network of brain regions, including the hippocampal region, in the processing of memory-related value signals.
source: Neurally, this possibility is consistent with evidence supporting the interplay between memory and choice processes, which involves a network of brain regions, including the hippocampal region, in the processing of memory-related value signals (Barron et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2015; Palombo et al., 2015; Weilbächer and Gluth, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The drift rate in sequential sampling models reflects the quality of information drawn from stimuli during the evidence accumulation.
source: Past theoretical and empirical work has suggested that the drift rate in sequential sampling models reflects the quality of information drawn from stimuli during the evidence accumulation (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Ratcliff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A higher drift rate is associated with recognizing an item that has been previously presented multiple times relative to an item presented only once.
source: Within the domain of memory, a higher drift rate is associated with recognizing an item that has been previously presented multiple times relative to an item presented only once (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Gluth et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Memory that is selectively reactivated during sleep renders higher quality evidence signals in favor of the cued item, giving rise to behavioral shift toward items previously named during sleep.
source: The correlation between drift rate biases and WTP biases observed in our data thus indicates the intriguing possibility that memory that is selectively reactivated during sleep renders higher quality evidence signals in favor of the cued item, giving rise to behavioral shift toward items previously named during sleep.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: The behavioral shift observed may reflect the modulatory effect of memory on attention, which in turn biases preferences and choices at the time of decision-making.
source: A second but not mutually exclusive possibility is that rather than playing a direct role in affecting value computation and comparison, verbal cueing initiates a chain of events that exerts modulatory effects on the decision process. For example, the behavioral shift observed in our data may reflect the modulatory effect of memory on attention, which in turn biases preferences and choices at the time of decision-making.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation.

claim: Eye fixation or cue-approach training has been shown to influence decisions through attention.
source: In line with this hypothesis, recent evidence based on either eye fixation (Krajbich et al., 2010) or cue-approach training (Schonberg et al., 2014; Bakkour et al., 2017) has suggested the influence of attention on decisions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: If individuals pay more attention to better-remembered options, preference enhancement following selective memory reactivation during sleep may reflect an increase in attention due to improved memory consolidation.
source: Consequently, if individuals pay more attention to better-remembered options, preference enhancement following selective memory reactivation during sleep may reflect an increase in attention due to improved memory consolidation (Chun and Turk-Browne, 2007; Goldfarb et al., 2016; Rosen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Sleep likely represents a unique period during which preferences and choices that are otherwise stable can be selectively modified by external cues.
source: The results of the present study suggest that sleep likely represents a unique period during which preferences and choices that are otherwise stable can be selectively modified by external cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Targeted memory reactivation not only benefits memories of newly acquired information but can also be used to eliminate long-standing social biases.
source: This finding is consistent with past evidence that targeted memory reactivation not only benefits memories of newly acquired information but can also be used to eliminate long-standing social biases (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There is evidence for the capacity of neurocognitive processing of verbal stimuli during N2, including extracting information from incoming words.
source: On the one hand, there is evidence for the capacity of neurocognitive processing of verbal stimuli during N2, including extracting information from incoming words (Kouider et al., 2014), differentiating their motivational saliency (Blume et al., 2017), and reactivating the existing motor or vocabulary memories associated with the words (Kouider et al., 2014; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is evidence for the capacity of neurocognitive processing of verbal stimuli during N2, including differentiating their motivational saliency.
source: On the one hand, there is evidence for the capacity of neurocognitive processing of verbal stimuli during N2, including extracting information from incoming words (Kouider et al., 2014), differentiating their motivational saliency (Blume et al., 2017), and reactivating the existing motor or vocabulary memories associated with the words (Kouider et al., 2014; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is evidence for the capacity of neurocognitive processing of verbal stimuli during N2, including reactivating the existing motor or vocabulary memories associated with the words.
source: On the one hand, there is evidence for the capacity of neurocognitive processing of verbal stimuli during N2, including extracting information from incoming words (Kouider et al., 2014), differentiating their motivational saliency (Blume et al., 2017), and reactivating the existing motor or vocabulary memories associated with the words (Kouider et al., 2014; Schreiner and Rasch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is wealth of evidence on TMR during slow-wave sleep in humans.
source: On the other hand, it is also possible that our results are not restricted to the period of light sleep, given the wealth of evidence on TMR during slow-wave sleep in humans (Rasch et al., 2007; Rudoy et al., 2009; Antony et al., 2012) and the entire non-rapid eye movement sleep in rodents (Rolls et al., 2013; Barnes and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is evidence on TMR during the entire non-rapid eye movement sleep in rodents.
source: On the other hand, it is also possible that our results are not restricted to the period of light sleep, given the wealth of evidence on TMR during slow-wave sleep in humans (Rasch et al., 2007; Rudoy et al., 2009; Antony et al., 2012) and the entire non-rapid eye movement sleep in rodents (Rolls et al., 2013; Barnes and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: According to the active system consolidation model, sleep-dependent memory consolidation critically relies upon repeated reactivation of memory representations.
source: According to the active system consolidation model, sleep-dependent memory consolidation critically relies upon repeated reactivation of memory representations (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Rasch and Born, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Following overnight sleep, subjects demonstrate an overall increase in favorable perception of the whole choice set, due to enhanced recalls for positive information associated with choice options.
source: For example, there is evidence that, following overnight sleep, subjects demonstrate an overall increase in favorable perception of the whole choice set, due to enhanced recalls for positive information associated with choice options (Karmarkar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Midday nap produces no general effect on either the overt behavior or computational parameters reflecting the latent cognitive processing directly related to decision.
source: In the present study, however, midday nap produces no general effect on either the overt behavior or computational parameters reflecting the latent cognitive processing directly related to decision.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data.

claim: The beneficial effect of sleep on memory consolidation requires sufficient sleep duration and the presence of slow-wave sleep.
source: One possibility is that the beneficial effect of sleep on memory consolidation requires sufficient sleep duration and the presence of slow-wave sleep (Backhaus and Junghanns, 2006; Diekelmann et al., 2011; Diekelmann et al., 2012), whereas daytime naps usually consist of lighter sleep stages such as stage 1 and 2 (Backhaus and Junghanns, 2006; Tucker et al., 2006; Genzel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Daytime naps usually consist of lighter sleep stages such as stage 1 and 2.
source: One possibility is that the beneficial effect of sleep on memory consolidation requires sufficient sleep duration and the presence of slow-wave sleep (Backhaus and Junghanns, 2006; Diekelmann et al., 2011; Diekelmann et al., 2012), whereas daytime naps usually consist of lighter sleep stages such as stage 1 and 2 (Backhaus and Junghanns, 2006; Tucker et al., 2006; Genzel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous research shows similar effects of memory stabilization following either 40-min sleep with TMR or 90-min sleep without external stimulation.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, previous research shows similar effects of memory stabilization following either 40-min sleep with TMR or 90-min sleep without external stimulation (Diekelmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Simple choices are fundamental for goal-directed behavior and have served as a cornerstone for studying reward and motivational control across species.
source: More broadly, simple choices are fundamental for goal-directed behavior and have served as a cornerstone for studying reward and motivational control across species (Fehr and Rangel, 2011; Padoa-Schioppa, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ninety-nine subjects were recruited by the Laboratory of Sleep Research at the Institute of Mental Health, Peking University.
source: Ninety-nine subjects were recruited by the Laboratory of Sleep Research at the Institute of Mental Health, Peking University (79 women, age = 23.42 ± 2.36; Supplementary file 1, Table 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: Seven subjects were excluded from the analyses due to insufficient variances in WTP1 (N = 3), a priori–defined insufficient nap time (N = 2), or being able to recall verbal stimuli in the post-sleep awareness test (N = 2).
source: Seven subjects were excluded from the analyses due to insufficient variances in WTP1 (N = 3), a priori–defined insufficient nap time (N = 2), or being able to recall verbal stimuli in the post-sleep awareness test (N = 2).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied to the sample.

claim: Subjects were randomly divided into sleep (N = 47) and wake (N = 45) groups.
source: Subjects were randomly divided into sleep (N = 47) and wake (N = 45) groups.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Sleep was recorded using polysomnography in all sleep group participants.
source: We recorded sleep using polysomnography in all sleep group participants, and cue-induced EEG signals in a subset of 23 sleep group participants (Supplementary file 1, Table 1D, Table 1E).
evidence: This describes the data collection methods.

claim: Cue-induced EEG signals were recorded in a subset of 23 sleep group participants.
source: We recorded sleep using polysomnography in all sleep group participants, and cue-induced EEG signals in a subset of 23 sleep group participants (Supplementary file 1, Table 1D, Table 1E).
evidence: This describes the data collection methods.

claim: All subjects were instructed to refrain from eating for 4 hr before coming to the laboratory.
source: All subjects were instructed to refrain from eating for 4 hr before coming to the laboratory and were provided with identical amounts of food upon arrival to ensure a minimal level of hunger.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Subjects were provided with identical amounts of food upon arrival to ensure a minimal level of hunger.
source: All subjects were instructed to refrain from eating for 4 hr before coming to the laboratory and were provided with identical amounts of food upon arrival to ensure a minimal level of hunger.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Subjects were not informed about the study hypotheses and did not know that they were going to receive any external stimulation while asleep.
source: Subjects were not informed about the study hypotheses and did not know that they were going to receive any external stimulation while asleep.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure to ensure blinding.

claim: Verbal cueing started 2 min after a subject displayed stable N2 sleep for the first time.
source: In the sleep group, verbal cueing started 2 min after a subject displayed stable N2 sleep for the first time and paused if there was any polysomnographic signal indicating microarousal, awakening, or entering other sleep stages.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Verbal cueing paused if there was any polysomnographic signal indicating microarousal, awakening, or entering other sleep stages.
source: In the sleep group, verbal cueing started 2 min after a subject displayed stable N2 sleep for the first time and paused if there was any polysomnographic signal indicating microarousal, awakening, or entering other sleep stages.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Wake group participants were kept awake for the same duration and were presented with verbal stimuli at approximately the same time when cues were delivered to sleeping participants.
source: Wake group participants were kept awake for the same duration and were presented with verbal stimuli at approximately the same time when cues were delivered to sleeping participants.
evidence: This describes the control condition procedure.

claim: Verbal stimuli were delivered via loudspeaker during auctions at intensity of 70 dB.
source: Verbal stimuli (duration range: 0.65–1.05 s, mean ± SD: 0.89 ± 0.08) were delivered via loudspeaker during auctions (intensity: 70 dB) and the verbal stimulation sessions (intensity: 55 dB).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Verbal stimuli were delivered via loudspeaker during the verbal stimulation sessions at intensity of 55 dB.
source: Verbal stimuli (duration range: 0.65–1.05 s, mean ± SD: 0.89 ± 0.08) were delivered via loudspeaker during auctions (intensity: 70 dB) and the verbal stimulation sessions (intensity: 55 dB).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: A low-intensity, 35 dB white noise was constantly delivered during sleep to block environmental noise.
source: A low-intensity, 35 dB white noise was constantly delivered during sleep to block environmental noise.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Verbal cues were delivered with intervals ranging from 4.5 s to 5.0 s during N2 sleep.
source: After sleep group subjects entered N2 as assessed by standard EEG criteria (Iber et al., 2007), verbal cues were delivered with intervals ranging from 4.5 s to 5.0 s.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each snack name was repeated for exactly 10 times in a row before presenting the next snack item.
source: To increase the chance of triggering memory replay in the sleep group, each snack name was repeated for exactly 10 times in a row before presenting the next snack item.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: For each subject, eight different snack names were presented in a randomized order.
source: For each subject, eight different snack names were presented in a randomized order.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Verbal stimulation was immediately paused when EEG recordings showed any signs of micro-arousal, awakening, or changing of sleep stages.
source: Verbal stimulation was immediately paused when EEG recordings showed any signs of micro-arousal, awakening, or changing of sleep stages.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: On average, cueing was interrupted 0.75 ± 0.58 times in the sleep group.
source: On average, cueing was interrupted 0.75 ± 0.58 (mean ±SD) times in the sleep group.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: Six scalp electrodes (C3, C4, F3, F4, O1, and O2) were placed according to the international 10–20 system and referenced to the contralateral mastoid.
source: Six scalp electrodes (C3, C4, F3, F4, O1, and O2) were placed according to the international 10–20 system and referenced to the contralateral mastoid, along with electrooculogram (EOG) and chin electromyogram (EMG) channels.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording methods.

claim: EEG signals were sampled online at 500 Hz with Profusion Net Beacon software.
source: EEG signals were sampled online at 500 Hz with Profusion Net Beacon software (Compumedics Sleep Study System, Melbourne, Australia) and filtered between 0.3 and 35 Hz.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording methods.

claim: EEG signals were filtered between 0.3 and 35 Hz.
source: EEG signals were sampled online at 500 Hz with Profusion Net Beacon software (Compumedics Sleep Study System, Melbourne, Australia) and filtered between 0.3 and 35 Hz.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording methods.

claim: Thirty second epochs were used for manual analysis of sleep stages.
source: Thirty second epochs were used for manual analysis, and periods of wakefulness, N1, N2, N3, and REM sleep were identified offline by two independent raters based on standard criteria from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) (Iber et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the sleep staging methods.

claim: Periods of wakefulness, N1, N2, N3, and REM sleep were identified offline by two independent raters based on standard criteria from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
source: Thirty second epochs were used for manual analysis, and periods of wakefulness, N1, N2, N3, and REM sleep were identified offline by two independent raters based on standard criteria from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) (Iber et al., 2007).
